title: Partition Tree
section: Where would a regression tree put its prediction?
text:
Where would a regression tree put its prediction?







A CART split groups observations by xx. Look at the 12 points in the shaded leaf.
In classification, class frequencies give us a probability for each label.

In squared-error regression, the prediction is the leaf mean, 2.75. What does it tell us about the gap?



Ask for a prediction before revealing the line. Every observation in this leaf is either below 1 or above 3. The mean is a good answer to a squared-error question. If we want to know what a future outcome might look like, the empty space between the bands matters too.

title: Partition Tree
section: A probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)
text:
A probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)



Andrei Kolmogorov
Foundations of the Theory of Probability, 1933








Kolmogorov’s 1933 framework gives discrete and continuous probability the same starting point. The sample space Ω\Omega lists the possible outcomes. The sigma-algebra ℱ\mathcal F specifies the measurable events, and PP assigns their probabilities. Point to the dot. Any point in the square can be the outcome ω\omega.
On the first click, treat each tile as a block of outcomes. “Did the point land in either shaded tile?” is one event. Each tile contains infinitely many points and is an atom of this σ\sigma-algebra. Choosing which of the 16 tiles to include gives 2162^{16} events.
On the second click, read the ruler from left to right in the same order as the tiles, row by row. Segment length shows probability. The shaded tiles have equal area but carry different masses. Since they are disjoint, their probabilities add.
For a continuous example, keep the same square, choose its Borel σ\sigma-algebra, and let probability be uniform area. Now each singleton is an event of probability zero, while the whole square has probability one. Countable additivity is consistent with that because the square contains uncountably many points.

title: Partition Tree
section: One die, three levels of information
text:
One die, three levels of information
Roll a fair six-sided die. The sample space is always Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.



What we learn
Blocks of outcomes
Measurable events




ℱ0\mathcal F_0 · No face information
Ω\Omega
2


ℱ1\mathcal F_1 · Odd or even
{1,3,5},{2,4,6}\{1,3,5\},\ \{2,4,6\}
4


ℱ2\mathcal F_2 · Exact face
{1},{2},…,{6}\{1\},\ \{2\},\ \ldots,\ \{6\}
64




Measurable events are unions of these blocks, called atoms. Finer atoms give ℱ0⊊ℱ1⊊ℱ2\mathcal F_0\subsetneq\mathcal F_1\subsetneq\mathcal F_2.


Parity lets us ask if the roll was even, with probability 1/21/2. The exact face lets us also ask if it was 22, with probability 1/61/6.


With one atom, ℱ0={⌀,Ω}\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}. With two atoms, ℱ1\mathcal F_1 also contains the odd and even events. With six singleton atoms, ℱ2=2Ω\mathcal F_2=2^\Omega. These collections contain Ω\Omega and are closed under complements and countable unions. The fair-die measure sums the 1/61/6 masses of the faces in each event. If we reveal the parity first and then the exact face of the same roll, the nested sigma-algebras form a filtration.

From a partition to a tree




Start at the root, the whole square. Each fork cuts the current rectangle in half. Follow the teal path through four cuts to reach tile AA. The orange path ends at BB. Our event is the union of those two leaves. Here we chose the cuts by hand. Where would a tree cut if it learned from the data?

title: Partition Tree
section: What if we also split the outcome?
text:
What if we also split the outcome?







Keep the same xx-band. Make one cut at y=3y=3.

Nine observations fall in the top unit of height. Three occupy the lower three units.


Per unit of outcome space, the upper cell is nine times as dense.



Give the audience a moment to count. The lower cell holds a quarter of the mass over three quarters of the height. Each rectangle will get one density. A further split could distinguish the little cluster near zero from the gap above it.

title: Partition Tree
section: Which split should the tree make?
text:
Which split should the tree make?







The parent assigns density 1/41/4 throughout the band.

After the cut, the upper density is 3/43/4. The lower density is 1/121/12.


Score each observation by the change in its log density. For this cut, Ĝ=9log⁡3+3log⁡(1/3)20≈𝟎.𝟑𝟑.\widehat G
=\frac{9\log 3+3\log(1/3)}{20}
\approx \mathbf{0.33}.



The parent density is 12 divided by the product of 12 and 4. In the upper cell the density triples. In the lower cell it falls to a third of the old value. The eight points on the right have no change in score. The denominator is twenty because this gain is measured per training observation across the whole tree. These are natural logarithms, so the gain is in nats per observation.

title: Partition Tree
section: Growing a Partition Tree
text:
Growing a Partition Tree
Try each admissible XX or YY split in each current leaf. Compare the two children with their parent using the same gain.
Ĝ(A→L,R)=∑B∈{L,R}nXY(B)Nlog⁡ĉBĉA\widehat G(A\to L,R)=
\sum_{B\in\{L,R\}}\frac{n_{XY}(B)}{N}
\log\frac{\widehat c_B}{\widehat c_A}

Split the leaf with the largest reduction in the training log-loss surrogate. Repeat until the split budget is spent or no admissible split remains.


Sorted thresholds need one scan per coordinate. For balanced growth, the paper gives O(dZNlog⁡N)O(d_Z N\log N) with maintained presorted indices, the same order as presorted CART.


An x-cut changes which observations supply the covariate denominator. A y-cut keeps that denominator and changes the outcome volumes. The gain uses unnormalized leaf heights, which makes it local. A priority queue keeps the best split available at every leaf. Here d_Z counts the splittable input and outcome coordinates. Sorting afresh within each node gives the balanced-tree comparison O(d_Z N log² N). These are training costs.

title: Partition Tree
section: Predicting with Partition Tree
text:
Predicting with Partition Tree








Given (x,y)=(0.25,3.5)(x,y)=(0.25,3.5), follow one branch at every split. The leaf height here is 3/43/4.

Given only x=0.25x=0.25, follow the matching branch at each XX-split and both branches at each YY-split.


The slice is a histogram. Its two bin areas are 3×(1/12)=1/43\times(1/12)=1/4 and 1×(3/4)=3/41\times(3/4)=3/4.



Trace the diamond, then click and trace the vertical line. For this particular tree the areas already sum to one. In general, leaves on a slice can have different covariate denominators. Divide all heights by the sum of height times outcome volume to obtain a proper conditional density. A normalized point query also needs this factor, which can be obtained from the slice. Integrating the histogram then answers probability and quantile questions.

Two modes can trade probability mass

text:
Almost-sure L1L^1 consistency
Theorem 3.2. Under these conditions, the conditional density estimate converges.
∥f̂πN−f∥L1(ν)→0almost surely,ν=PX⊗μY.\bigl\|\widehat f_{\pi_N}-f\bigr\|_{L^1(\nu)}\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \nu=P_X\otimes\mu_Y.
Assume i.i.d. sampling from PXY≪νP_{XY}\ll\nu, admissible leaves, finite VC dimension for leaf XX-projections, and finite-volume outcome truncations with vanishing tail mass.

Maximum leaves in one tree m(𝒜N)=o(N)m(\mathcal A_N)=o(N).
Maximum groupings of the same NN points log⁡ΔN*(𝒜N)=o(N)\log\Delta_N^*(\mathcal A_N)=o(N).
Mass in large leaves vanishes as the sample grows.
PXY{z∈𝒵‾N:diam⁡(πN[z])>γN}→0P_{XY}\{z\in\bar{\mathcal Z}_N:\operatorname{diam}(\pi_N[z])>\gamma_N\}\to0 a.s. for some γN→0\gamma_N\to0.
Maximum distinct XX-regions in one tree mX(𝒜N)log⁡N/N→0m_X(\mathcal A_N)\sqrt{\log N/N}\to0.

Angelim & Leite, Theorem 3.2

The norm integrates absolute density error over outcomes with respect to μY\mu_Y and over covariates with respect to PXP_X. Every leaf AA has positive empirical covariate mass and positive outcome volume. The outcome truncation 𝒴‾N\bar{\mathcal Y}_N has finite μY\mu_Y measure, and its excluded probability tends to zero almost surely. We write 𝒵‾N=𝒳×𝒴‾N\bar{\mathcal Z}_N=\mathcal X\times\bar{\mathcal Y}_N.
The family 𝒜N\mathcal A_N contains the possible output partitions. For condition 1, count the leaves in each partition and take the largest count. For condition 2, hold a sample of NN points fixed and count the distinct groupings these partitions induce on it. A grouping counts once even if several partitions produce it. The growth function takes the largest such count over all samples of size NN.
Condition 3 says that the total probability in leaves larger than a shrinking diameter threshold tends to zero. Large leaves can persist with vanishing probability mass. Diameter measures continuous spread after a bounded monotone transform and unresolved categories. For condition 4, project each leaf onto XX, count each distinct region once, and take the maximum over possible trees. For example, the two leaves from the earlier YY-split share one xx-band and contribute one region.
Theorem 3.2 concerns the piecewise-constant estimate in Equation (11). Corollary C.4 gives the same convergence after slice normalization. Proposition C.5 controls conditions 1, 2, and 4 when the split budget is o(N/log⁡N)o(\sqrt{N/\log N}). For the greedy rule used in the benchmarks, Proposition C.8 gives shrinkage with a growing split budget under the paper’s gain-margin assumption.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
text:
Code is not meant to be written once and never touched again. It is meant to be read, understood, and modified over time. This is especially true in dynamic environments, where requirements change, new features are added, and bugs are fixed. In such environments, code design quality is not just a nice-to-have; it is essential for the long-term success of the project.
Here, I wish to share some thoughts on code design qualities, focusing on what we want, not how to get there. This is not a guide on how to write good code but rather a reflection on what good code design means in the context of software engineering and data science. This can also be useful for managers, product owners, and stakeholders who do not code but want to understand how quality impacts the product they are building.
The key takeaway I wish you to have is that good code design is about resilience. It is about not overfitting to our myopic view of the present, but rather about crafting a solution that can adapt and generalize to future requirements, just like a good machine learning model. It is about how effortless it is to adapt to changes.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
section: The map is not the territory
text:
The map is not the territory





There is this nice quote from Alfred Korzybski that says “the map is not the territory”. This means that any representation of reality is not reality itself, but rather a simplification of it. Also, it is shaped by our biases and limitations.
Bringing it to the context of this post, we can say that product requirements are not the product we are building. They are a simplification of what we want to build. Naturally, details can be missing and assumptions can be wrong, because sometimes reality is more complex than what we can express in words. Sometimes, we just don’t know, and that is okay. We just have to be cautious not to mistake the empty with the void.
This idea is key to understanding what comes next. Our code is designed to solve problems, but our definitions of problems are not perfect. They are made by humans, and hence this human aspect and the imprecise understanding of what should be done is deeply connected to the quality of the code we write, even more so than what our linter and unit tests end up being.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
section: Easy is not simple
text:
Easy is not simple
Before using the word “simple” to describe code, we should properly define what we mean by that. As gloriously explained by Rich Hickey in his talk “Simplicity Matters,” simple is not the same as easy. Simple is about not packing together unrelated concerns; it is about giving clear responsibility to each component, and making it easy to modify and extend. Easy, on the other hand, is subjective; it is what is closer to your knowledge and experience, it is what you are used to doing, and not necessarily good. We should focus here on the code, not on our perspective of knowledge and experience.
This definition aligns with the one in the book “A Philosophy of Software Design” (Ousterhout (2018)), which is a huge inspiration and reference for this post.

Complexity is anything related to the structure of a software system that makes it hard to understand and modify the system

Complexity is not related to the number of lines or functions; it is about the bigger picture. In his book, John Ousterhout also enumerates some symptoms of complexity:

Change amplification: when a change in one part of the system requires changes in many other parts.
Cognitive load: when the code is hard to understand, requiring a lot of mental effort to comprehend.
Unknown unknowns: when it is hard to diagnose where a change is needed to complete a task.

Basically, simplicity implies less effort in the long term.
Think about the code as a graph. The nodes are components (e.g., functions) we create, and the edges represent their dependencies. Simple code would be a graph with few edges, where edges represent dependencies of components on others. A dependency can be, for example, an assumption of the structure of the output of one component, the existence of certain methods, etc. The number of edges would be proportional to the complexity of the system and our cognitive load.





If we would perturb the graph above, such as changing the output of node 11, it would only affect the nodes that are directly connected to it, and not the whole graph. This is what we want to achieve with our code: a graph with few edges, where we can easily replace parts without affecting the whole system.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
section: The objective function
text:
The objective function
Here, I’ll try to define a conceptual “objective function”—not mathematical, but rather a guiding principle that should shape how we design and structure our code.

Overfitting to training data
At first glance, you might think that code is good if it simply does what it’s supposed to do. However, this perspective often encourages quick-and-dirty solutions and spaghetti code that might solve immediate problems but overlook the bigger picture.





Imagine an abstract space of requirements, like the one above. We can only see a tiny fraction of our long-term goals clearly. Focusing too narrowly on the present moment—what we already know—makes us overfit to our current understanding, limiting our ability to adapt to new challenges. The more complex and specifically tuned code is, the more likely it is to overfit and struggle when things inevitably change.





While “easy” solutions may feel quicker and simpler initially, generalizable, well-designed solutions usually save more effort in the long run. They avoid the exponential increase in complexity and maintenance costs that come from constantly adapting overfitted solutions.







The regret
I’ve often wondered what exactly we’re optimizing for when designing and writing code. Just like machine learning models use metrics to evaluate their performance, we need something to measure code quality. After some thought, I’ve come to see regret as a useful measure.
In simple terms, regret is the extra effort spent compared to an ideal solution. This concept is borrowed from machine learning, particularly from the “multi-armed bandit” problem, where decisions must be made based on limited information. The goal there is to minimize regret—the gap between your choices and the best possible outcomes—over time. This mirrors how we write code, making choices with incomplete information and constantly adapting as we learn more.
Experienced developers naturally have lower regret because they anticipate changes more effectively, ask better questions early on, and build resilient systems from the start.







Good code starts before writing code
Since we rarely have full information upfront, we shouldn’t aim for perfect code immediately. Instead, the first thing we should do is ask questions:

What requirements are likely to change?
What requirements are unlikely to change?
What assumptions are we making?
What is the expected lifespan of the product?

With the answers to these questions, we can start shaping our design. Once we have a draft proposal, we can evaluate how different possible future changes would affect the current structure.





Designing often involves identifying stable components and defining contracts between them. Asking the right questions early helps us group functionalities meaningfully and build systems that remain flexible over time.


Avoid premature optimization
While it’s important to anticipate change, guessing too far ahead about possible future requirements can be dangerous. This is known as premature optimization. It can create significant regret—first due to excessive effort upfront, and later because reality rarely matches our early guesses.





I once found myself in this trap: trying to optimize a codebase that wasn’t even in production yet. I went deep into SOLID principles, endlessly splitting functions and abstracting for flexibility I thought I might need later. But those future requirements never arrived. The code became so abstract that it was hard to maintain, and when real changes eventually came, I had to rewrite everything anyway.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
section: Conclusion
text:
Conclusion
Writing good code isn’t just about making something that works today — it’s about building solutions that can adapt, evolve, and scale as requirements inevitably change. Much like training a machine learning model, if we overfit our code to the present, we may pay a heavy price in the future. Balancing simplicity, flexibility, and pragmatism is what leads to resilient systems with low long-term maintenance cost.
By focusing on minimizing regret—the extra effort caused by early design decisions that don’t age well—we can make smarter choices even when information is incomplete. And while experience helps us make better bets, asking the right questions early on dramatically increases our odds of success.
In the end, it’s not about writing perfect code — it’s about writing code that can gracefully survive its own future.

title: Can your code pass the test set?
section: Key Takeaways
text:
Key Takeaways

Code quality is about resilience, not just correctness
Overfitting code to today’s requirements creates fragile systems.
Minimize regret: optimize for adaptability, not hypothetical future needs.
Good design starts with asking the right questions, not jumping into abstractions.
